newsitem.title: USA: Florida official says Prudential blocked probe.
newsitem.headline: Florida official says Prudential blocked probe.

text.p: Florida Insurance Commissioner Bill Nelson on Monday charged Prudential Insurance Co of America with obstructing a state probe into allegations that the company misrepresented its insurance policies as investments.
Nelson filed a formal administrative complaint alleging that the company obstructed the investigation, destroyed documents and ignored subpoenas.
Nelson's office began an investigation in April 1995 into allegations that the company churned accounts and misrepresented some policies as investments.
He said the allegations stretched over at least 14 years and may involve more than 100,000 Florida policyholders.
The insurance commissioner said that unless the company provided the requested documents, it could face sanctions possibly including loss of its license to operate in Florida.

"By my order today, I'm putting the burden on Prudential to show why I should not impose the stiffest of fines or revoke or suspend its license to do business in Florida," Nelson said at a press conference in Tallahassee.
As insurance commissioner, Nelson is authorized to revoke or suspend if a company's sales practices are proven injurious to Florida consumers.

Florida Attorney General Bob Butterworth said his department was also investigating the company. "We will pursue all the options available to us to ensure that all those who suffered are fairly compensated," Buterworth said.
"That will include the RICO act as well as civil theft," he said, referring to the state's Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organization Act.
Holding up a full-page advertisement in the Sunday edition of the New York Times, Butterworth said Prudential used consumer confidence in the company to deceive mostly elderly policy holders.

"When they talked about selling you 'a piece of the rock,' then they go ahead and hit you over the head with it," Butterworth said. "A piece of the rock" is Prudential's longstanding advertising theme line.

Florida is one of only a handful of states that have not agreed to setttle with the Newark, N.J.-based insurance company over charges that its agents throughout the 1980s misrepresented its products and sold insurance policies as investments.

Butterworth also accused the firm of persuading policyholders to use the current value of their policies as collateral to purchase other products, enabling the agents to earn additional commissions. The practice is known as "churning."
Earlier this year, Prudential reached an agreement with 43 other states to pay a $30 million fine and set up a fund for policyholders who could prove they were churned by the company's agents.

The company has also agreed in a separate $410 million class-action lawsuit that it would reimburse policyholders for similar practices. That case is still pending before a federal judge in New Jersey.
Nelson and Butterworth said they would file objections seeking to block the settlement in the New Jersey case. A hearing is scheduled January 21 before a federal judge in New Jersey.
"This settlement is a bad deal for policyholders. It does not begin to compensate Florida consumers whose pockets were picked," Nelson said.
The Florida officials said Prudential sold plain life insurance policies to elderly people by pitching them as tax-favored investments or "inflation safety nets."
Nelson said he would give the "benefit of the doubt" to Arthur Ryan, the newly appointed chief executive of Prudential, in the hope the company would begin cooperating with Florida investigators.
Prudential is the largest of a number of insurance companies to be charged with such practices nationwide in recent years.
